p: Thank you. Thank you so much, Chair Lee. Wow, we have a full house today. We have almost enough members to hold a Stated Meeting and have quorum. So a few questions. I'll start my question—
We attract a crowd.

I'll start my questions on the topic of large-scale events. As we know, we're one month away from the World Cup in July. With increased tourism coming to New York City for the FIFA World Cup, you issued a memo stating that officer shifts will be 12 hours from July 1st to

July 7th. How exactly will this work? Are they expected to work three days per week for a total of 36 hours and then a half of a shift for 40 or 42 hours?

No. They will either work pre-tour or post-tour overtime. So importantly for our officers, during that week, we are not throwing out their chart. They will continue to work their standard five days a week, just with four hours added either to the beginning or to the end of their tour. And the Chief of Department is going to soon issue guidance to each bureau about how their 12-hour tours are going to work, meaning are they doing pre-tour or post-tour. Chief, do you have anything to add to that? Okay.
All right, so five days a week, 12-hour tours.

Five days a week, 12-hour tours, but in that time we are doing things like canceling training. We are canceling all things that could otherwise be a drain on NYPD resources. We do not expect to be canceling their RDOs, their

regular days off, as a practice. It may have to happen from time to time.
Is this going to apply to every police officer?

We're not going to cancel, for example, like, if they have holiday picks, they're not going to have to work, you know, when they were planning to be away. But it is going to apply to the vast majority of— well, I'd say the majority of police officers in the New York City Police Department for that week, and perhaps for a few days closer to the finals, will be asked to work 12-hour tours. And that is from the rank of police officer on up to, to chief. So it really affects everyone. It is not a decision that we took lightly, or that I took lightly, but it is an absolute necessity for that week given the number of things going on in that– in the city.
Approximately how many police officers would this apply to? You said a vast majority. Would you say more than 80 percent? 80, 90, ballpark?

I don't want to give an actual percentage. What I can say is that the Chief of Department is going to issue guidance to each bureau and once we have that guidance, we will let your office know what percentage it applied to.

How much overtime is projected for that week of the World Cup? Can you give the numbers? Well, for the World Cup or the July 1st to July 7th? Because, like, remember, we've got July 4th, Sail 250, which is like, the President's military parade in New York City, NBA Finals, World Cup, all as potentially Taylor Swift's wedding. I'm kidding. But all as overlapping events in New York City between June 11th and July 19th. Any one of those on their own would be a big deal in New York City. All of them taken together are unprecedented and are going to place unusual and I would say historic demands on the New York City Police Department. So Kristine, can you go through the July 1st to July 7th, what that dollar value projection is, and then also for the World Cup specifically?

So these projections are preliminary, but for the July 1st

July 7th, our projection order of magnitude is that will cost between $35 to $42 million for that period overall for FIFA and Sail 250. So this entire time of all of these overlapping events, we believe overtime is projected about $73 million on top of that. Obviously there's equipment that the department needs to make sure that we're able to keep everything safe, secure, and also also manage the crowds. That's $12.4 million. And then there's $6.5 million for drone equipment. So in total, the estimate right now is $92 million. The good news is that the budget that you've all looked at already really accounts for on the city side about $50 million, and then there's another $21 million in federal funding. So there's $71 million that we're accounting for. All the federal funding is not quite reflected yet, but that does leave a shortfall of about $20 to $21 million based on projections.

I will just add that the federal government/FIFA did not give us nearly enough money to cover the overtime bill on the New York City Police Department. Kristine, how much did FIFA give us, $14 million?
So they gave us $14.6 for the overtime, toward overtime, and $6.5 for counter-drone equipment. We are having conversations about potentially getting more, but that's not determined yet.
It's gonna be a rough start to the fiscal year for our overtime. Just remember that for next year's overtime hearings.
We'll keep that in mind. Talk to us about the plan for fan safety at transit hubs and also watch parties?

The plans— okay. So with all of these major events that are going on in New York City, there will be other joyful events going on around them in New York City. All of those events will require a police presence. For example, NBA Finals watch parties, FIFA watch parties, people taking the subway, using mass transit, going to and from those watch parties, people going to the events themselves, meaning getting people to the— from New York City to the World Cup is a whole to-do in and of itself that requires security. They're going mostly by bus or by rail, and there's a big screening

component and security component there. So, it would be an understatement to say that we have been planning. We have been, like, aggressively planning for so many different things that are occurring this summer, not just the main events themselves, but all of the festivities surrounding those events. And remember, FIFA is an international name and therefore a target. And so we do not look at FIFA as just a normal event in New York City. Both the FIFA tournament and the events surrounding FIFA in New York City, the fan zones, the watch parties, those we all have to look at seriously through the counterterrorism lens.
Speaking about events, how will the NYPD work with federal and state authorities to ensure participants are safe getting to and from the events?
Hand in hand. The Chief can— do you want to talk through the buses and the trains and how you're coordinating with partners on that?

Sure. So on the eight game days at MetLife, there– we have identified four

separate locations that over 200 buses will be starting in New Jersey, swept in New Jersey with an NYPD presence to make sure that they are swept properly. Those buses then come into New York City. Obviously, we're not able to park 200 buses in and around the four identified areas, so we will start with 45 buses at a time. That footprint at those locations start 12 hours prior to those buses being parked there. Obviously, those locations have to be swept by our counterterrorism team. They then have to be— the footprint has to stay there until the buses actually arrive. Those buses, each one of those buses, I've assigned two uniformed officers to, again, to continue to observe those buses to make sure that, you know, they're safe to go back into New Jersey. Again, very dynamic. The 42nd Street will be the street that we will be using that will be closed to just bus and emergency vehicles going through the tunnel into New Jersey. As far as the rails, we have identified approximately, we think, upwards of 15,000 people to go through Penn Station and then ultimately have to get screened by the NYPD to go again into New Jersey. So it's a huge– it's a huge undertaking. On

top of doing all that, on the eight game days, there will be numerous watch parties throughout New York City. And, you know, again, we've gone from 32 teams to 48 teams. We've gone from approximately 150 games to 200 games. Every game that is being played will be front and center in New York City. As far as the rails, working with our federal partners and Amtrak. So actually, next week I will be chairing a meeting with the northeast corridor from— from Washington, D.C. up to and through New York City with Amtrak, MTA, and all our rail partners to make sure that, again, it's seamless, it's safe, and the federal government, the state government, and obviously the NYPD are working very, very close.
Thank you, Chief.

Speaking about the World Cup and also watch parties, there's been numerous articles which stated that public events, including World Cup watch parties on open streets and plazas and parks will be scaled back due to NYPD concerns. Is it true? And if yes, can you talk to us about some of the concerns? And also, is the plan or

the hope to have police presence at every single watch party?

My understanding is that the Mayor is going to announce a very robust set of watch parties for FIFA around all five boroughs, which will run the length of the tournament. We do have, that we know of, already announced the five FIFA fan zones that will be– five FIFA fan zones, one in each borough. So my hope and my expectation is that we are going to have a lot of festivities in New York City around the World Cup. Obviously, we need— we want to celebrate. We need to celebrate safely. I already told you about the need to look at all things FIFA through a counterterrorism lens. That's what this department is doing. We don't have unlimited resources, and we also have a lot of other things that are occurring in New York City. You know, when a country hosts the World Cup or the Olympics, usually they cancel everything else going on in that city at that time. We didn't in New York City. We're still having— we're having the Puerto Rican Day Parade. We're having lots of— the Pride Parade. We are having many or nearly all of the standard large-scale events

in New York City this summer that we would have in a summer with, like, none of these events going on. And so I would appreciate it if you could think about the demands on this department in that context. We would like to facilitate a lot. Perhaps we won't be able to facilitate everything, but there will be a lot of celebrating in New York City.
So, absolutely, yes. And of course, we're going to— we're expecting there to be a lot of requests for permits for watch parties in communities and etcetera. And on that issue–

And just know that for each one, the– for each city-sponsored one, the Chief and Commissioner Weiner have to put together a full counterterrorism package because again, that name FIFA comes with elevated threat.

Right. Yes. And of course, there's a lot of agencies that play a role when it comes to issuing permits. NYPD plays a big role in reviewing and issuing them. What are factors that the NYPD will consider when determining whether to issue let's say, a watch party on Fordham Road?

Whether we— so whether we can do it safely, which means does the footprint make sense? Can we secure it appropriately with blocker cars? Like, we don't want cars driving into these watch parties either on purpose or by accident. We don't wanna be— we've seen vehicle ramming attacks across the city. Do we have the resources available to it? Like, for example, are there several other watch parties going on in the same precinct at the same time? So, I mean, the main thing is, are we able to ensure a responsible amount of security at the event?
What are areas that are more likely to receive an approval for a watch party? I'm sure doing a watch party at a park would be much easier to secure, you know, it's more difficult to—

Usually it is. That is true. Each permit application we review based on the specific details. So, how big is it? Where is it? Is it in a heavily trafficked area? Is it right near a subway station? Does it run right alongside of busy corridor where a vehicle can just come right up into

it? Like, there are so many different factors that we look at. What else is going on in the city at the same time? I mean, everyone needs to remember we have a day in New York City where we both have a— hopefully or potentially an NBA Finals game in New York City and a World Cup game in the New York/New Jersey area. So we also have to look at what's going— what else is going on in the city that day.

All right, thank you for the information. So I'll ask some questions about the overtime issue, and then I know my colleagues have a lot of questions, so then I'll pause there. So can you repeat the numbers related to overtime, let's say, for the last seven years, the last seven fiscal years? And for these questions, let's just focus on the fiscal years because, of course, calendar years are very different from fiscal years.
Yeah, okay, sure. This– the fiscal— okay, at fiscal year 26, the first three quarters, we are projected to be down 10 percent in overtime spend.
What about total? Not just the first three quarters, total fiscal—
[interposing] Well, we're not— we do the— we're in the last quarter now.
Right? But projected for the last quarter included.

Oh, the projection is $1.013 billion, which is $91 million less than fiscal year 25, the same first three quarters. But for the first three— sorry, which is $91 million less than fiscal year 25. So the full year projection is $1.013 billion, $91 million less than fiscal year 25. For the first three quarters that have been completed in fiscal year 26, we are down 10 percent in overtime compared to the first three quarters of fiscal year 25. And if you take out the transit overtime, which the Governor pays for, and you put overtime spend in today's dollars, meaning in today's contract dollars, how much the cops are paid, the FY26 overtime spend is projected to be six percent lower than that historical average going back to 2016.
And what has been the total overtime budget since, let's say, 2020, all of the fiscal years since 2020?
Yeah, I can get– I can get you that.
I have it here. It's this chart here, Kristine, right?
Yep, those are the adjusted values. Yep.
You go ahead.
Yeah, so going back to 2020, so if you look at, again, excluding the transit, it was a billion in fiscal year 2020.
Well, including the entire thing, transit, the entire—
Well, with transit, there wasn't really much transit that year.
There wasn't transit–

So that was a billion for, like, billion— it was basically a billion in fiscal year '20. Fiscal year '22 was $576, but that was basically because of the pandemic, so that's really an outlier. Fiscal year 22 was $918, fiscal year 23 was $1,047,000,000, fiscal year 24 was $1,155,000,000, and fiscal year 25 was $1,128,000,000.
But fiscal year 25 is when transit started.
Correct?
And so if you take transit out, which the governor pays for, then fiscal year 25 is $954, and the projection for FY '26 without transit is $862.
Correct.

So I know it's a big spend for overtime, but I just want to make sure that the members of this council understand that his— like, if you look at historical spending totals, the numbers here seem more reasonable than they otherwise would.

Yeah, and that is my next question. Why are we still spending $1 billion in overtime? I mean, you know, I know all of you continue to mention that the previous administration, there was an anything-goes system. There were—
[interposing] There was, and that's why—
[interposing] Significant changes, and that–
[interposing] Yeah, there was.

If I could just finish— and there were also about 4,000 new police officers added last year, which exceeded attrition rates. So I'm just curious, why are we still in the ballpark of $1 billion? This is something that we don't see with any other agency.

Yeah. So the officers that were added last year, the reason we hired 4,000 of them is because 20 years ago we had hired huge number of officers. So we hired four— over 4,000 officers last year to make sure that we kept up with attrition. In fact, we beat attrition by a few hundred officers, which was a minor miracle. But I don't want to give the impression that we ended the year up 4,000 officers. We ended the year up several hundred officers, which is the first time we'd ended the year up for many years. At the same time, it is the case that before I got here, the Department did not manage overtime in any meaningful way. And it, to me, looked like when I showed up an anything-goes system. And the executive team here under the First

Dep and the Deputy Commissioner of Management and Budget’s leadership have put in, I think a very responsible overtime plan that has delivered meaningful results— a 10 percent decline in overtime in fiscal year 26 and a 12.4 percent decline in overtime in calendar year 25. And we will continue to do that. As to the question about why overtime is required, I think we need not look farther than what's going on this summer and the previous questions you just asked. Are we going to be able to have all of these watch parties? Are New Yorkers going to be able to celebrate? And the answer is, like, yeah, we're going to do a lot of celebrating. But that celebrating needs to be safe. And in order for it to be safe, we need to make sure that we have officers there and that we have thought through all of the security requirements. So for things, for example, like special events, that requires overtime. For protests, things that are, like, unexpected, that requires overtime. Sometimes, for example, like, if we're seeing a gang war in the 44, and we say, the officers on Saturday night, they usually end at— I'm making this up— at one in the morning or midnight and

we want them to stay on post till two in the morning because we want to make sure that we curb the gun violence. Those are examples of things that we would use overtime for.

Right, absolutely. And, yes, this is as we know, this is– is and will always be a very busy city. New York City will always have large-scale events, also sports events, parades, and etcetera. But I think the big— and of course we need and appreciate the police presence at these events to make sure that people are safe. But the big question, or the big point here, is whether there's any measures that we can take so that we could have that police presence, let's say, for example, by increasing headcount and not have to continuously rely on $1 billion of overtime.

I do not believe– having more officers this summer would definitely decrease the overtime, the need for overtime this summer for all of these special events, and in my opinion, could have an overall general effect on overtime. But those are budget decisions that the council needs to make in coordination with the mayor

and his team. I am doing the best I can with the officers that we have, and I am very pleased that so far this year, in his first month, the mayor has given us over 500 additional officers budgeted for the New York City Police Department, 580.
Brief question on headcount. So the headcount is approximately 35,000. What percent of this 35,000 is patrol officers versus community affairs and any other units?

Oh, I have that. Hold on one second. Oh, here it is. Our patrol staffing, I'm very pleased to tell you, is 888 officers. As of April 30th this year, 888 officers over what it was the same time in 2025. So we have nearly 1,000 additional officers on patrol now. If you compare April 30th of this year to April 30th of last year, and that our number right now, I believe, is 15,749. I wanna be clear, those numbers include our evidence collection teams, and our domestic violence units. So I'll just explain why. Historically, so last year and the year before and the year before that, forever, those two teams were part of our Patrol Services

Bureau. So they were included as part of the patrol headcount. They have been moved now to be under the Detective Bureau, but they perform the same functions that they performed when they were under Patrol Services. So I'm giving you an apples-to-apples comparison.
All right. A few–
[interposing] And the Bronx is up 250 officers. I know you care about that since last year.
Thank you for that. We'll take– thank you so much for that. We’ll take more of those.

You're about to get more. That's the great thing about all the hiring we did last year. Now, we do 18 months of training for these officers on the street. And as they hit that 18 months, they go into precincts where they're responding to 911 jobs. So every few months now, precincts across the city are going to see an influx of new police officers on patrol, and it is something now that we can enjoy for the next year, and so long as our great hiring continues.

Thank you. Thank you so much for that. And we're absolutely seeing the results. I've been around a few incidents and the police response has been at the speed of light. So that's something that we appreciate and we welcome. A few more questions about the issue of overtime. What are the top three things that lead to overtime? I'm sure large-scale events is going to be something big this year. Protests–
Large-scale events. Do you have that, Kristine?

Yeah, so, it's events, it's investigations, and then basically we have the other categories are roughly even with arrests, operational, crime reduction, and then of course we have our transit safety as well. But the two largest areas are investigations and the events.

All right. And just two more questions. I know we have a lot of colleagues who have signed up for questions. A few– a question about officer deployment. Approximately how many officers do we have for a large protest versus a

smaller protest, also large-scale events, and also for parades, a smaller parade versus a larger parade? What's the ballpark of a lot of officers?
It really runs the gamut. It just– it varies so much that it is hard to answer that question. Do you wanna—

Sure, I can answer it. Let's just just look at yesterday's parade. So yesterday's parade— and this is total uniform members, so I'm not separating our CT teams, I'm not separating our emergency service— we had over 3,000 officers that were assigned to that detail. And again, we look at security risks, we looked at— we look at past incidents, not just in New York City but across the world. And we also look at, you know, how many participants we expect at those events. So a lot of times it could be hundreds of officers, but many times it could be thousands of officers.
And the same is true for protests. It just really depends on how many people are expected to go to the protest, where is the protest, what time of day, what else is going on, all of those factors.

If I may also just— the tiered system that we have in the protest element speaks to this as well, right? So, it's everything that the Chief of Department was just saying, the Police Commissioner was saying, and then one thing that has been a product of the protest settlement is thinking through, okay, how many officers do we actually need to do this responsibly, appropriately, consistent with the settlement? And I think that's actually been a real benefit of the protest settlement.

All right, thank you for the information. Final question before I pass it on to colleagues. And on the issue of overtime, I'm sure there's a lot of things that— a lot of ways that we could get to overtime. Let's say a police officer has to work a few additional hours after their shift. They can also do overtime during their, as they say, RDOs, during their regular day off. They're off and they're called to work. What percentage of overtime hours are worked by officers already working versus those that are during their RDOs they're supposed to be on.
We’re going to have to get that to you. We don't have that data right here, but I think that we can figure that— get that number for you.
Okay, thank you. So I'm going to pause here. We could get that. I know you have your team here. We could get that through my next round. That would be—

[interposing] I don't think we're gonna be able to get that in the next round. The Deputy Commissioner of Management and Budget will get it over to your office, but she's got to do a little work to get that number out.
Okay. Thank you.
Okay, perfect. So we have Deputy Speaker followed by Councilmember Cabán.

Hello, Commissioner. Just a quick question about something you said in your testimony around hate crimes. You had mentioned that it was down 5.4 percent, but we saw some reports that show a jump to 11.8 percent, and that rapes are also up. So just wanted to know if you can explain, like, the differences between, like,

your testimony and some reports that we saw that says—

[interposing] Yes, the reports that you saw reference the first quarter of– the numbers at the end of the first quarter of the year. So January, February, March. The numbers that I gave account for April as well. And so it changed. You know, these are– hate crime is a terrible thing, but these are small-ish numbers compared to overall crime. So a few crimes can make a big difference in terms of up or down.

Thank you. Just turning questions to the racial equity plans that you put forward. I've been asking all city agencies about their racial equity plans, especially during budget hearings, because we hope that budget allocations are being appropriated to fulfill some of the goals. So one of the goals of the NYPD is to enhance the hiring process by removing unnecessary barriers, bringing greater transparency to decisions, and ensuring qualified candidates are not excluded by the system. This is listed as a short-term goal to be completed by 2026. Has the department done a review

in the past of the hiring process? What was the outcome of this review? And is any funding in this budget going towards recruitment and hiring?

So there have been many reviews of the hiring process, but I’m not one that particularly looks at equity. So the hiring panel is convening over a period of about 100 days. It met earlier last month in the initial meeting. It's a collection of experts, academic experts, community members really across the board to give us their best thoughts on how to improve that process. So we had our initial kickoff. We should have our next meeting I think in just a couple of weeks, and then we'll have a final meeting at the end and those are where the recommendations will come out of. There's no funding allocated just for the study, that's just being done with in-house staff.

And just to answer the last part of the question, a lot of the success that we have had in hiring over the past year and a half has been driven by our fraternal organizations. So those fraternal organizations going out into their communities, educating people about the work of

police officers. We– a year ago at this time, we're— we couldn't find enough candidates to take the job. You know, we had an actual— our actual headcount was well below the budgeted headcount. And I give the work of those– those fraternal organizations, a lot of credit for the work that they have done getting people interested in the job.
Thank you. Another goal is to increase representation in leadership positions and specialized units by 2028. Which units currently have the lowest levels of diversity?
I have to get back to you. We can get back to you with the diversity by unit.

Okay, just turning over to some district-specific questions. So I appreciate the Q teams. I visited each Q team in my district. We love them. But some of the things that– I see Chief Obe here– specifically around truck parking and making sure that these precincts have the resources to remove trucks and address a lot of the overnight commercial vehicle parking in residential

neighborhoods. So just wanted to know specifically about her division and the budget there and how you—
Which division?
The Chief Obe.

Oh, Chief Obe. So what I want to say on that is I think the paradigm that this department has used forever on towing makes no sense. And the precincts that have heavy towing needs should probably have tow trucks assigned to them and people trained in how to use them assigned there as well. That is what makes sense for me. You know, Council Members always wanna give us funding for strategic things, and I think that if we can reorganize appropriately, that might be a great new way to address some of the acute towing problems that we are seeing in specific precincts, including in yours–
Yes, I love that idea. And I know, like, all of us in Southeast Queens would definitely allocate— I hear sound effects—
[interposing] So we'll have to—
to our precincts, because we do try to support them. Like, I know—
let's have conversations–
[interposing] Okay.
about we can make that a reality. I think that that will be more meaningful than talking about how much money is assigned to the Transportation Bureau. But, Kristine has that for you.
It's $212 million.
Okay.
Thank you.

So just on a final note, just to add, in your district, since we met with you, the work still continues. On 10 dates we had— we wrote 259 summonses 51 tows so far, and 51 boots also. So the work will continue.

Okay, thank you. Just one more question about my favorite

division in the police department, which is the Community Affairs Division. I would love to see— every year I ask for an increase because there are, like, amazing community affairs officers. One precinct, they're doing a whole dance recital, you know, and they do the best that they can. They raise money inside of the police department. They externally ask for resources, but I feel like when I think of, like, community policing and what we all want to see from the police department, I feel like this is, like, the unit that does that work.
Yep.

And I feel like they just don't— I would love to see them have more money. You know, the game truck breaks down, the rock wall, there's only, like, one rock wall. Would love to see a rock wall in each bureau. I mean— This is just my yearly, please give more money to the Community Affairs Division.

Noted. I hear you on that. I will say that one thing that we have done, and this was at the request and advice– on the advice of virtually every precinct CO that I have spoken to.

For four years, the Community Affairs Officers were not assigned to their precincts. They were reassigned to a centralized Community Affairs Bureau, which basically meant that the precinct CO lost his or her basically right-hand person, but particularly, definitely the right-hand person for dealing directly with the community, because that person no longer reported to him and her. As of January this year, I was very pleased to reassign Community Affairs officers back to their specific precincts, and I think that that has and will continue to go a long way. There are still many Community Affairs officers that are centrally assigned under the Community Affairs Bureau, but I think restoring that function under patrol has led to some very positive outcomes. And I am getting positive feedback on that, both from many of your colleagues, but just as importantly, many precinct COs that I speak to.

We've also been joined by Council Member Banks, and we'll go with Council Member Cabán, followed by Wong. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Thank you. As always, I have lots of questions, so I'm going to ask

that y'all be as succinct as possible. I'm going to start with just some money numbers. Can you tell me FY 26 to date the money spent on the Quality of Life Division, and if you could break that down to like money spent on the the Q teams, QStat, and then just the projected budget for FY 27 for those?
Kristine has that for you.

So I'm actually have to get back to you because I don't have a broken back by each bureau by spend-to-date. So I will get back to you on that. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay. That would be really helpful. Are you tracking complaints and civil suits based on the– that particular division's enforcement?
Like CCRB complaints? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And civil suits.
And what? COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: And civil suits, yeah.
Civil suits.
So, if the question is, do we sort of have like a separate tracking system by division? I mean, we certainly can pull that data. That's not— there's data that we can get. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay.

But I don't think that we're tracking it sort of day-to-day sort of by division. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Okay. So I want to move on to different questions. I think the request is, can you pull the data on that and provide it to the Council in terms of the complaints and civil suits coming out of Quality-of-Life enforcement?
Yes. For sure. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Great. Thank you.
Out of the Quality of Life Division. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: The quality of life division. Yes.

Yep. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: What– Commissioner, what evidence does the NYPD have that

increased arrests for low-level offenses improve public safety outcomes?

To be clear, we are not looking to make increase arrests for low-level offenses. We give our officers a huge amount of discretion. Discretion starts with engagement. The Quality of Life Division was certainly not created to gin the number of low-level arrests. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: Well, Commissioner, that's not my question. I don't— no, but that's not my question, so I just want to redirect for a second. The— what evidence does the NYPD— because we have it in prior hearings where you have testified and others?
I don't have evidence. I don’t have evidence of it, because that is not a stated goal, so I wouldn't look at that. COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: No–
[interposing] The stated goal of the Quality of Life Division– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Okay.
is to address the explosion of quality of life complaints that we have seen across– COUNCIL MEMBER CABÁN: [interposing] Okay.
